messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
David is a 57-year-old tutor who came to treatment after years of arranging his life around not being caught off guard. The assault happened when he was in his forties. He described being cornered by another man in a private setting and overpowered, the worst part not only the sexual violation but the moment he realized he could not stop what was happening. What has stayed with him most sharply is the combination of forced physical contact and the absolute loss of control over his own body. Even now he can say certain sensory details with painful precision—the feel of a hand pinning him, the closeness of a male body, the trapped certainty that saying no made no difference—while other parts seem to fall away. He knows there are missing pieces, and when he tries to explain the event aloud, he often stops, frustrated, saying he knows what happened but cannot find words for it.

In the months afterward, David did not simply feel upset; he came to believe the world had changed into a place where safety depended on constant caution. He was certain he had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. That belief settled alongside another, more painful one: that his own body had become unreliable, something that had failed to protect him and could not be trusted to warn him in time. The memories fed that conclusion. Their clarity made the assault feel undeniable and close, but the blank spaces left him feeling even less secure, as if danger could come from what he did not fully remember as much as from what he did. Over time he also felt increasingly set apart from other people, especially from other men, as though he had been pushed into a private world no one else could quite enter.

Those meanings now shape what catches him in daily life. Because he has come to expect danger and to doubt his own capacity to stay safe, physical touch startles him immediately, being directed or pressured by someone can feel intolerably charged, and being alone with a man is often enough to make his body tense before anything has actually happened. At the tutoring center where he works, he pays close attention to who is in the room and where they are standing. If a male student arrives early and he finds himself alone with him, David begins scanning for signs of threat in the student’s posture, tone, and movements. When parents or staff reach out casually to pat his shoulder in thanks, the contact can pull up the assault with startling force: a vivid flash of the physical restraint, followed by the sickening sense that parts of the memory are still out of reach. In those moments he feels again how little he trusts his body, and the old conviction returns that he is fundamentally alone in managing this.

The memories and the sense of current threat now reinforce each other. The more closely David watches other people for signs they might harm him, the more readily details of the assault spring up. He chooses seats in waiting rooms, classrooms, and coffee shops with almost ritual precision, always locating the chair that feels most protected and gives him the clearest view of the room. He avoids unfamiliar places because he cannot quickly assess the danger there. That constant surveillance leaves him primed; a man standing too near in a hallway, an unexpected brush of arms, or a situation in which someone else seems to be deciding for him can bring back the assault in sharp fragments. Each resurgence of memory confirms his belief that the threat is still immediate and that vigilance is necessary, while each episode of vigilance seems to sharpen the memory again.

From those beliefs, a pattern of coping has narrowed his life. Because he feels isolated, unable to trust his body, and convinced that strong emotion will overwhelm him, David avoids situations likely to stir much feeling. He keeps conversation with students focused tightly on coursework and declines social invitations from colleagues. He has become notably rigid about physical boundaries, stepping back from handshakes or finding ways to keep a desk between himself and others. Smoking has become another way he manages the internal surge; he describes slipping outside between sessions not for pleasure but to settle himself, to do something familiar when his chest tightens and his thoughts start racing. His monitoring of exits and strangers makes him choose routines over spontaneity, and his avoidance of touch has affected even benign contact, contributing to a life that feels controlled but increasingly small.

What finally brought him in was a recent incident at work when a male student, trying to show him something on a screen, leaned in and touched his forearm. David froze, lost the thread of the lesson, and afterward sat in his car chain-smoking, shaken by how immediately the memory had returned and how complete his fear felt. He was frightened by how powerfully these moments still govern him and by the possibility that he will keep retreating from work and from people until there is very little left. At the same time, he said quietly that he hopes for something simple: to sit in a room without calculating danger, to teach without bracing for touch, and to feel that his body belongs to him again.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows triggers bringing up memory and threat, but it does not state that triggers themselves lead David into negative appraisals or beliefs.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette explains that negative appraisals shape what catches him in daily life, but it does not explicitly convey that those appraisals generate or heighten triggers/reminders themselves.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: Although memories are said to feed earlier conclusions and confirm threat, no paragraph clearly states that trauma memories directly produce David’s negative appraisals in the present.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows threat reinforcing memory and driving vigilance and avoidance, but it does not explicitly state that the sense of threat leads to negative appraisals or distorted beliefs.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Those meanings now shape what catches him in daily life. Because he has come to expect danger and to doubt his own capacity to stay safe, physical touch startles him immediately, being directed or pressured by someone can feel intolerably charged, and being alone with a man is often enough to make his body tense before anything has actually happened.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each time one of these moments catches him, the same conclusion lands with it: that he is still vulnerable, still unable to trust his own body to protect him, and still largely on his own with this.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
In the months afterward, David did not simply feel upset; he came to believe the world had changed into a place where safety depended on constant caution. He was certain he had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Once he saw ordinary life through that lens, more and more things began to snag his attention as possible warnings; a man lingering in a doorway, an unexpected touch, even being alone in a room no longer felt neutral enough to ignore.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He knows there are missing pieces, and when he tries to explain the event aloud, he often stops, frustrated, saying he knows what happened but cannot find words for it.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
When those sharp fragments break through, they leave him thinking not just that the assault was terrible, but that something in him remains damaged and unreliable if the memory can still seize him so completely.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The memories and the sense of current threat now reinforce each other. The more closely David watches other people for signs they might harm him, the more readily details of the assault spring up.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Living in that level of alarm has itself become proof to him that his life is no longer fundamentally safe and that he is not someone who can afford to let his guard down.
<<<END>>>
